eras.pages: Pages 155-159, 297-333, 380-387 (and references in star catalogue section pp 592-654)

eras.name: Nabonassar
eras.detail: Era Nabonassaris: Epoch at 26 February 748 BCE (year 0). Named after Babylonian king. Used for Egyptian calculations in vague years (365 days without intercalation). Also called 'Bukhtanaşşar' by Arabs. Base reference era for most other calendar conversions.

eras.name: Seleucid / Dhū l-qarnayn (Alexander the Bicorn)
eras.detail: Era Seleucidarum (also called Aera Alexandri Dhú 'l-qarnayn): Epoch Friday 1 September 312 BCE (some sources say 1 October). 11 Julian years 10 months 26 days (or 11 years 9 months 3 days) after Nabonassar. Uses Julian calendar year (365.25 days). Interval: 12 Egyptian years between start of Seleucid and Alexander of Macedon death eras.

eras.name: Philip of Aridaeus (Philippi Aridaei)
eras.detail: Aera Philippi Aridaei: Epoch Friday 12 November 324 BCE. From death of Alexander the Great ('a morte Alexandri'). Uses vague Egyptian years (365 days). Interval from Seleucid: 4311 vague days = 11 years 10 months 26 days. Also used as 'Macedonic' epoch in Theon's Manual Tables.

eras.name: Augustus (Coptic)
eras.detail: Aera Augusti vel Actiacae: Epoch Friday 29 August 25 BCE (following Theon's interpretation). An 'Alexandrian' form with Julian calendar years. Epoch sometimes given as 30 August 30 BCE in other sources. Interval from Seleucid: 287 Julian years minus 3 days.

eras.name: Diocletian / Martyrs
eras.detail: Aera Diocletiani vel Martyrum: Epoch Friday 29 August 284 CE. Used by Coptic Christians (still in use in modern Egypt). Julian calendar. Mentioned in calculations of trepidation (p. 386-387) with interval of 313 years after Augustus.

eras.name: Hijra (Arabs / Hegira)
eras.detail: Aera Hegirae: Epoch Thursday 15 July 622 CE (astronomical reckoning) or Friday 16 July 622 CE (civil reckoning). Lunar calendar with alternating 30 and 29-day months; year = 354 11/30 days. Interval from Seleucid: 932 Julian years before Hijra began. Conversion formulas given in detail (pp. 156-159).

eras.name: Yazdegerd (Persian)
eras.detail: Aera Iazdegerdis (Yazdaģird filii Shahriyār): Epoch Tuesday 16 June 632 CE (start of reign of Yazdegerd III). Persian calendar with 12 months of 30 days plus 5 epagomenal days = 365 days exactly. Interval from Seleucid: 943 Julian years. Interval from Hijra: 3624 days (about 9-10 years).

eras.name: Coptic (Greek-Egyptian)
eras.detail: Aera Coptorum (Graeco-Aegyptiorum or Theonian): Epoch Friday 1 September (year 1 CE in Theon's system, but al-Battani uses modified epoch). Uses vague Egyptian calendar (365 days). Interval from Seleucid: 287 Julian years. Coptic calendar months: tūt, bābah, hatur, kiyahk, tūbah, amshir, barmahāt, barmūdhah, bashans, bawūnah, abib, misri (each 30 days + 5 epagomenal days).

eras.notes: FOUND CONTENT: Comprehensive chronological material in the Nallino Latin edition. Primary discussion in Pars II, Cap. XXXII-XXXIII (pp. 297-333) where al-Battani explicitly treats the conversion of multiple eras (Nabonassar, Seleucid, Philip, Augustus, Diocletian, Hijra, Yazdegerd, Coptic). The material is partly technical prose and partly tabular. Pages 155-159 contain detailed conversion algorithms and calendar month names for all major eras. Pages 330-331 show a table with era names in multiple languages/scripts (including Arabic and other columns). Pages 380-382, 386-387 discuss era applications to astronomical calculations and trepidation theory. The text is in Latin (Nallino's translation/commentary of al-Battani's Arabic original). Key numeric intervals are provided: Nabonassar to Seleucid = 12 years; Seleucid to Hijra = 932 years; Hijra to Yazdegerd = 3624 days; other intervals explicitly stated in pages 157, 297-298, 330, 332-333. No 'Flood' era appears in this Latin volume (may be in the original Arabic but not translated in Nallino). Material includes explanation of calendar systems, month names in Coptic/Greek/Arabic, and detailed epoch dates.

kings.notes: Canon of Kings (Tabulae regum peregrinorum) extracted from al-Battani's Opus Astronomicum as preserved in C. A. Nallino's critical Latin edition (Pars II, 1910). This is al-Battani's chronological Canon used for astronomical calculations, listing rulers from six major dynasties: Babylonian/Assyrian kings (Nabonassarus era), Persian Achaemenids, Hellenistic successors (Alexander and Ptolemaic Egypt), Roman emperors, Byzantine Christian emperors, and Islamic caliphs (with dates in Islamic calendar: years/months/days). The table closely follows Ptolemy's chronological framework as referenced in the Almagest. For Islamic caliphs, the years are given in Islamic lunar years with months and days. This Latin edition represents the state of the Arabic/Syriac original; some rulers' names show textual variants or corruptions noted in the critical apparatus at pp. 639-642.
